catalog_quote: Plains Apache has a register tone system with two levels, low and high. Low is written with a grave accent (e.g. bìs, 'bank'), and high is written with an acute accent (e.g. šéł, 'kindness'). Syllables with short vowels bear a single toneme, but those with long vowels have one toneme for each mora of the vowel, making for a total of four contours: high-high, tʼǫ́ǫ́š, 'bark'; high-low, béè-lą̀ą̀ʔ, 'point'; low-high, gòóʔ, 'snake'; low-low, gààd, 'spread of cedars'

new_statements.quote: In the Apachean sub-stock are found six mutually unintelligible idioms: Navaho, San Carlos, Chiricahua-Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, and Kiowa-Apache. The following remarks on pitch accent apply with equal force to each of these languages [...] An utterance in the Apachean languages, phonetically considered, is a succession of evenly stressed syllables each of which possesses a clearly defined pitch accent or tone. [...] there are no distinctive accentual patterns characteristic of the word, the phrase, or the sentence which stand over and above the accentual patterns formed by the succession of syllables constituting the utterance.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; this supplies the deciding statement: tonal, no distinctive word stress, syllables evenly stressed. The statement is made explicitly for all six Apachean languages including Kiowa-Apache, but the illustrative forms are Navaho ('All of the examples quoted here.. are, unless otherwise stated, from Navaho', fn. 3, p. 39).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kiowa-Apache, like the other five Apachean languages, has syllable tonemes (four: high, low, falling, rising; the inflected tones only on long vowels or vowel clusters) and no word-level stress: syllables are evenly stressed and there is no distinctive accentual pattern of the word over and above the tones of its syllables. Tone is the only prominence feature; the paper then gives morphophonemic rules for tone (neutral-toned morphemes take low tone, with assimilation before high-toned syllabic n).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none; all syllables described as evenly stressed
new_statements.exceptions: only for tone assignment (neutral-toned syllables assimilate to a following high-toned syllabic n, p. 40); no exceptions to the no-word-stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Both Hoijer papers call the language 'Kiowa Apache' / 'Kiowa-Apache' (abbreviated K.A.), spoken 'in northern Texas' per 1938 (the Oklahoma community; = Plains Apache, kiow1264). Hoijer 1938 places it alone in the Eastern group beside Jicarilla-Lipan and states the K.A. data are his own unpublished fieldwork. The 1943 stress/tone statement is pan-Apachean: asserted 'with equal force' for Kiowa-Apache but illustrated with Navaho forms, so the Plains Apache reading rests on Hoijer's explicit extension rather than on K.A. examples.
